notes.definition: Some properties of hydrocarbons depend on the size of their molecules: as the number of carbon atoms increases, boiling point and viscosity increase and flammability decreases. Hydrocarbons are used as fuels because their combustion releases energy; in complete combustion the carbon and hydrogen are oxidised to carbon dioxide and water.
explanation: Hydrocarbons with different sized molecules behave differently. Three properties are linked to molecule size: boiling point, viscosity and flammability. As the hydrocarbon chain gets longer (more carbon atoms), the boiling point increases, so small hydrocarbons such as methane are gases at room temperature and larger ones are liquids or solids. This is because larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces between them, which need more energy to overcome.

Viscosity is how thick a liquid is, or how easily it flows. Long-chain hydrocarbons are more viscous: they are thick and flow slowly, like the heavy fuel oil or bitumen near the bottom of the column. Short-chain hydrocarbons are runny, with low viscosity, like petrol. Flammability is how easily a substance catches fire. Small hydrocarbons are very flammable and ignite easily; large hydrocarbons are harder to ignite and burn with a less clean flame.

These properties affect how hydrocarbons are used as fuels. A good fuel should ignite easily, flow easily through pipes and fuel injectors, and vaporise readily. This is why short-chain hydrocarbons such as petrol and LPG are in high demand as fuels, while very long-chain hydrocarbons are used for other purposes, for example in thick lubricating oils or bitumen for roads.

The combustion of hydrocarbon fuels releases energy, which is why they are burned in engines, boilers and power stations. Combustion is an exothermic reaction with oxygen. During combustion the carbon and hydrogen in the fuel are oxidised: they gain oxygen. In complete combustion, which happens when there is plenty of oxygen, the only products are carbon dioxide and water. For example: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.

You should be able to write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of any hydrocarbon if you are given its formula. Balance carbon first (one CO₂ for each C atom), then hydrogen (one H₂O for every two H atoms), then count the oxygen atoms on the right and put the right number of O₂ molecules on the left. If this gives a half, double everything. For example, for propane: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O.
keyFacts: As molecule size increases, boiling point increases.
As molecule size increases, viscosity increases (thicker, flows less easily).
As molecule size increases, flammability decreases (harder to ignite).
Short-chain hydrocarbons make better fuels: they flow and ignite easily.
Combustion of hydrocarbon fuels releases energy (it is exothermic).
During combustion, carbon and hydrogen are oxidised.
Complete combustion of a hydrocarbon produces carbon dioxide and water only.
Balance C, then H, then O; double all numbers if you end with a half.

keyTerms.definition: The temperature at which a liquid turns into a gas throughout; it increases with hydrocarbon chain length.
How thick a liquid is and how easily it flows; high viscosity means it flows slowly.
How easily a substance catches fire (ignites).
A reaction in which a fuel reacts with oxygen and releases energy.
Combustion with a plentiful supply of oxygen, in which a hydrocarbon produces only carbon dioxide and water.
Gain of oxygen; in combustion the carbon and hydrogen atoms are oxidised.
A substance that is burned to release energy.

workedExamples.title: Balancing a combustion equation (no halves)
workedExamples.question: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of pentane, C₅H₁₂.
steps: Oxygen on the right: (5 × 2) + (6 × 1) = 16 O atoms = 8O₂.

workedExamples.title: Balancing a combustion equation (with a half)
workedExamples.question: Write a balanced equation for the complete combustion of butane, C₄H₁₀.
steps: Oxygen on the right: 8 + 5 = 13 O atoms = 6½O₂.
You cannot have half a molecule, so double everything: 2C₄H₁₀ + 13O₂ → 8CO₂ + 10H₂O.

workedExamples.title: Using boiling point data
workedExamples.question: Butane boils at −1 °C and pentane at 36 °C. Predict the state of each at 20 °C.
steps: At 20 °C butane is above its boiling point, so it is a gas.
At 20 °C pentane is below its boiling point (and above its melting point), so it is a liquid.
workedExamples.answer: Butane is a gas and pentane is a liquid at 20 °C.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think larger hydrocarbons are more flammable because they contain more fuel.
misconceptions.right: In fact flammability decreases as molecules get larger; small hydrocarbons ignite much more easily.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that boiling a hydrocarbon breaks the covalent bonds inside the molecules.
misconceptions.right: In fact boiling overcomes the weak forces between molecules; the covalent bonds inside each molecule stay intact.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write that combustion produces 'carbon dioxide and hydrogen'.
misconceptions.right: In fact the hydrogen is oxidised too, so complete combustion produces carbon dioxide and water.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think viscosity means how dense a liquid is.
misconceptions.right: In fact viscosity is how easily a liquid flows. Thick, slow-flowing liquids have high viscosity.

realWorld: Petrol (short chains) is runny and ignites easily, so it is used in car engines with spark plugs.
Long-chain, viscous hydrocarbons are used as lubricating oils and bitumen for road surfaces rather than as fuels.
Gas boilers burn methane (natural gas) to heat water and homes; good ventilation ensures plenty of oxygen.
examTips: Learn the three trends as a set: bigger molecules, higher boiling point, higher viscosity, lower flammability.
In combustion equations, always balance C first, H second and O last.
Say that carbon and hydrogen are oxidised during combustion, not just 'burned'.
When reading a boiling point graph, compare each boiling point with room temperature (about 20 °C) to decide the state.
summary: Boiling point and viscosity increase with molecule size.
These properties decide which hydrocarbons are useful as fuels.
Complete combustion oxidises C and H to CO₂ and H₂O.
Balance combustion equations C, then H, then O.

questions.question: What happens to the boiling point of alkanes as the number of carbon atoms increases?
questions.explanation: Larger molecules have stronger forces between them, so more energy is needed to separate them and the boiling point is higher.

questions.question: What does 'viscosity' describe?
options: How easily a liquid catches fire
How hot a liquid gets when it burns
markScheme: 1 mark: how easily a liquid flows
questions.explanation: A viscous liquid is thick and flows slowly. Catching fire is flammability.

questions.question: What are the products of the complete combustion of a hydrocarbon?
questions.explanation: With plenty of oxygen, carbon is oxidised to CO₂ and hydrogen is oxidised to H₂O.

questions.question: Which hydrocarbon is the most flammable?
questions.explanation: Flammability decreases with molecule size, so the smallest molecule, propane, is the most flammable.

questions.question: Which hydrocarbon would be the most viscous?
questions.explanation: Viscosity increases with chain length, so the longest chain, C₃₀H₆₂, is the thickest.

questions.question: During combustion, what happens to the carbon and hydrogen in a hydrocarbon fuel?
questions.explanation: Carbon and hydrogen gain oxygen to form CO₂ and H₂O, which is oxidation.

questions.question: Which is the correctly balanced equation for the complete combustion of methane?
questions.explanation: Right side: 2 O in CO₂ + 2 O in 2H₂O = 4 O atoms, which is 2O₂. Hydrogen: 4 on each side.

questions.question: In the balanced equation C₆H₁₄ + xO₂ → 6CO₂ + 7H₂O, what is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Oxygen atoms on the right: 12 + 7 = 19, so 19 ÷ 2 = 9½ O₂. Doubled, the equation is 2C₆H₁₄ + 19O₂ → 12CO₂ + 14H₂O. 19 is the number of O atoms, not O₂ molecules.

questions.question: Why do hydrocarbons with larger molecules have higher boiling points?
options: The intermolecular forces between larger molecules are stronger
questions.explanation: Boiling separates whole molecules; covalent bonds inside molecules are not broken. Larger molecules attract each other more strongly.

questions.question: Balance this equation for the complete combustion of ethane by finding the number of carbon dioxide molecules, a: 2C₂H₆ + 7O₂ → aCO₂ + 6H₂O
questions.explanation: There are 2 × 2 = 4 carbon atoms on the left, so 4CO₂. Check O: 14 on the left; 8 + 6 = 14 on the right.

questions.question: Propane burns completely: C₃H₈ + xO₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Calculate the value of x.
questions.explanation: 10 oxygen atoms on the right means 5 O₂ molecules on the left.

questions.question: 16 g of methane burns completely in 64 g of oxygen. Calculate the total mass of carbon dioxide and water produced.
questions.explanation: No atoms are created or destroyed, so the total mass of products equals the total mass of reactants: 80 g.

questions.question: Octane burns completely: 2C₈H₁₈ + yO₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O. Calculate the value of y.
questions.explanation: 50 oxygen atoms on the right, so 25 O₂ molecules. Check H: 36 on each side; C: 16 on each side.

questions.question: The boiling points of hexane (C₆H₁₄) and octane (C₈H₁₈) are 69 °C and 126 °C. Estimate the boiling point of heptane (C₇H₁₆) by taking the mean.
questions.explanation: Heptane lies between hexane and octane, so the mean gives a reasonable estimate: 195 ÷ 2 = 97.5 °C. The real value is 98 °C.

questions.question: State how the flammability of hydrocarbons changes as the size of the molecules increases.
questions.explanation: Large hydrocarbons are harder to ignite than small ones.

questions.question: Write a word equation for the complete combustion of methane.
markScheme: 1 mark: methane + oxygen on the left
1 mark: carbon dioxide + water on the right
questions.explanation: Methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. Oxygen is a reactant, which is often forgotten.

questions.question: Use the boiling points given to state whether propane (boiling point −42 °C) and hexane (boiling point 69 °C) are solid, liquid or gas at 20 °C.
questions.explanation: 20 °C is above propane's boiling point, so it is a gas. It is below hexane's boiling point, so hexane is a liquid.

questions.question: Write a balanced symbol equation for the complete combustion of methane, CH₄.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct formulae CO₂ and H₂O
questions.explanation: 1 C gives 1 CO₂; 4 H gives 2 H₂O; total 4 O atoms on the right, so 2O₂.

questions.question: Explain why petrol is a better fuel for cars than a fraction containing hydrocarbons with 30 carbon atoms.
markScheme: 1 mark: petrol is more flammable / ignites more easily
1 mark: petrol is less viscous / flows more easily (or vaporises more easily)
questions.explanation: Short-chain hydrocarbons ignite and flow easily; long chains are thick and hard to ignite.

questions.question: Write a balanced symbol equation for the complete combustion of butane, C₄H₁₀.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct products CO₂ and H₂O with 4CO₂ and 5H₂O per butane
questions.explanation: 13 O atoms are needed per butane, which is 6½ O₂, so the whole equation is doubled.

questions.question: Explain why hydrocarbons with longer chains have higher boiling points. Use ideas about forces and energy.
markScheme: 1 mark: longer chains have stronger intermolecular forces (forces between molecules)
1 mark: more energy is needed to overcome these forces
1 mark: covalent bonds within the molecules are not broken when boiling
questions.explanation: Boiling separates molecules from each other. Larger molecules attract each other more strongly, so more energy (a higher temperature) is needed.

questions.question: A hydrocarbon burns completely to form 6 molecules of CO₂ and 6 molecules of H₂O for each molecule burned. Deduce its formula and state whether it is an alkane.
markScheme: 1 mark: C₆H₁₂ (6 C from 6CO₂; 12 H from 6H₂O)
1 mark: not an alkane, since an alkane with 6 C would be C₆H₁₄
questions.explanation: Each CO₂ contains 1 C atom and each H₂O contains 2 H atoms, so the fuel is C₆H₁₂. It does not fit CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.

questions.question: Describe how boiling point, viscosity and flammability change as hydrocarbon molecules get larger, and explain how this affects their use as fuels.
markScheme: Indicative content: boiling point increases with size; viscosity increases with size; flammability decreases with size; small hydrocarbons ignite easily, flow easily and vaporise easily, so they are good fuels (e.g. petrol, LPG); large hydrocarbons are thick and hard to ignite, so they are less useful as fuels or are used for other purposes such as lubricants or bitumen.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): all three trends correct and clearly linked to use as fuels.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two trends stated with little link to fuels.
questions.explanation: Link each trend to a fuel property: ignition (flammability), flow (viscosity) and vaporising (boiling point).

questions.question:
A student compares two fuels: pentane (C₅H₁₂, boiling point 36 °C) and hexadecane (C₁₆H₃₄, boiling point 287 °C).
Compare the properties of the two fuels and write balanced equations for the complete combustion of each. Explain which is more suitable as a fuel for a camping stove.
markScheme: Indicative content: pentane has smaller molecules; lower boiling point, so it vaporises easily; lower viscosity, flows easily; more flammable, ignites easily; hexadecane is more viscous, less flammable, higher boiling point; C₅H₁₂ + 8O₂ → 5CO₂ + 6H₂O; 2C₁₆H₃₄ + 49O₂ → 32CO₂ + 34H₂O; both release energy and are oxidised to CO₂ and H₂O; pentane more suitable as it lights easily and burns readily (but its high flammability needs careful storage).
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed comparison of all three properties, both equations correctly balanced, and a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): comparison of at least two properties, at least one correct equation, and a conclusion.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, e.g. pentane is more flammable, with limited balancing.
questions.explanation: For hexadecane: 16 CO₂ and 17 H₂O per molecule need 32 + 17 = 49 O atoms, so 24½ O₂; doubling gives 2C₁₆H₃₄ + 49O₂ → 32CO₂ + 34H₂O.

questions.question: Butane has a boiling point of −1 °C. What is its state at 25 °C?
options: It depends on the size of the container
questions.explanation: 25 °C is above butane's boiling point, so butane is a gas. It is stored as a liquid in camping gas cylinders only because it is under pressure.

questions.question: Give one reason why hydrocarbons are burned as fuels.
markScheme: 1 mark: combustion releases (a lot of) energy
questions.explanation: Combustion of hydrocarbons is exothermic: it releases energy that can be used for heating, transport and generating electricity.

questions.question: Which gas is needed for a hydrocarbon to burn?
questions.explanation: Combustion is a reaction with oxygen. Carbon dioxide is a product, not a reactant.
